Battle of the Coral Sea. Fought in May nineteen forty-two between American and Japanese naval forces in the Coral Sea east of Australia, this battle marked the first naval engagement in which the opposing ships never came within sight of each other. All damage was dealt by carrier-based aircraft. Though tactically inconclusive, the U.S. victory prevented a Japanese amphibious invasion of Port Moresby and halted Tokyo's southern expansion.

The engagement occurred from May fourth to eighth, nineteen forty-two. It was the first naval battle fought entirely by carrier aircraft, establishing air power as the dominant naval weapon in modern naval warfare. The U.S. carrier Lexington was sunk and Yorktown damaged. The Japanese light carrier Shoho was sunk and fleet carrier Shokaku heavily damaged. These losses proved decisive—Japanese commanders called off their Port Moresby invasion operation, known as Operation Mo, due to carrier losses and operational uncertainty.

The battle was commanded on the American side by Admiral Frank Jack Fletcher in the Yorktown, while Japanese forces were under Admiral Takao Kurita. Neither side achieved a decisive tactical advantage, and each side lost approximately equal tonnage and aircraft. Yet strategically, the outcome halted Japanese expansion southward and boosted American morale after the shock of Pearl Harbor. The battle served as a prelude to the more decisive victory that would come one month later at Midway, setting the stage for the reversal of Japanese fortunes in the Pacific.
